SBM-02.8(a) Business Development program: A Small Business Administration program that helps firms owned by socially and economically disadvantaged people compete for federal contracts.
SBM-02.HUBZone program: A Small Business Administration program that gives firms located in historically underutilized business zones an advantage in winning federal contracts.
SBM-02.APEX Accelerator: One of a network of centers, formerly called Procurement Technical Assistance Centers, that teach businesses how to sell to government agencies.
SBM-02.USDA Rural Development: The part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture that offers loans, loan guarantees and grants to businesses in rural areas.
SBM-02.Export-Import Bank: The federal export credit agency, which helps American businesses sell abroad with export credit insurance, loan guarantees and loans.
SBM-02.National Association for the Self-Employ: A membership organization that gives self-employed people and very small businesses advice, resources and group benefits.
SBM-02.Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship: A nonprofit that teaches entrepreneurship to young people, especially in under-resourced communities, through school programs.
SBM-02.Kauffman Foundation: A private foundation based in Kansas City that funds entrepreneurship research and education programs.

SBM-03.Collect receivables faster: Getting customers who bought on credit to pay sooner, by sending invoices promptly and chasing overdue ones, so cash arrives earlier.
SBM-03.Cut expenses: Reducing what the business spends, for example by trimming overhead or finding cheaper suppliers, so less cash goes out.
SBM-03.Increase sales: Selling more, through promotion or new customers, so more cash comes in. It helps only if the sales are actually paid for promptly.
SBM-03.Raise prices: Charging more for each sale brings in extra cash without extra units to make, provided customers do not leave.
SBM-03.Reduce inventory: Holding less stock and selling off slow-moving items, which frees the cash that was tied up in goods sitting on shelves.
SBM-03.Delay payments to suppliers: Agreeing longer terms or paying bills on the due date instead of early, which keeps cash in the business for longer.
SBM-03.Offer early payment discounts: Giving customers a small price cut, such as 2 percent, if they pay an invoice within a few days, to bring cash in sooner.
SBM-03.Use a line of credit: Borrowing from a pre-arranged credit limit to cover short gaps between paying bills and receiving customers' money.
SBM-03.Require deposits: Asking customers to pay part or all of the price in advance, so cash is in hand before the work is done.
SBM-03.Lease instead of buy: Renting equipment for monthly payments instead of paying the full price at once, which spreads the cash outflow over time.
SBM-03.Charge late fees: Adding a penalty or interest to overdue invoices, which gives customers a reason to pay on time.
SBM-03.Forecast cash flow: Estimating in advance the cash expected in and out each week or month, so shortages are spotted early enough to act.
SBM-03.Tighten credit policy: Being stricter about which customers may buy on credit and for how long, for example by checking their credit first.
SBM-03.Sell unused assets: Turning equipment, vehicles or property the business no longer needs into cash.
SBM-03.Factor receivables: Selling unpaid customer invoices to a finance company at a discount to receive most of the cash immediately.
SBM-03.Refinance debt: Replacing existing loans with new ones at a lower interest rate or a longer term, which reduces the monthly payments.
SBM-03.Bring in investors: Selling a share of ownership in return for cash, which adds money without loan payments but gives up some control.
SBM-03.Build a cash reserve: Setting aside money in good months as a cushion to cover bills in slow months or emergencies.
SBM-03.Sell subscriptions: Charging customers a regular recurring fee, which makes cash arrive predictably, and in advance when they pay up front.
SBM-03.Accept electronic payments: Taking cards, online and mobile payments so customers can pay immediately instead of mailing a check later.
SBM-03.Reduce owner withdrawals: The owner takes less money out for personal pay, leaving more cash in the business.
SBM-03.Sale and leaseback: Selling an asset the business owns, such as its building, and renting it back from the buyer. The firm gets cash and keeps using the asset.

SBM-07.Theft: Loss of goods or money through stealing, whether by shoplifters, burglars or dishonest employees. It is classed as a human risk.
SBM-07.Fire: Damage to or destruction of the building, equipment and stock by fire, which can also close the business while repairs are made.
SBM-07.Lawsuit: A legal claim against the business, for example by a customer hurt on the premises or by a faulty product, which can bring large costs.
SBM-07.Natural disaster: An event of nature such as a flood, hurricane, tornado or earthquake that damages property and interrupts business. It is a natural risk.
SBM-07.Economic downturn: A recession or slump in which customers have less to spend, so sales fall. It is an economic risk the business cannot control.
SBM-07.New competition: A rival opening nearby or entering the market and drawing customers away, which reduces sales and may force prices down.
SBM-07.Employee injury: A worker hurt on the job, leading to medical costs, lost work time and possible claims. Workers compensation insurance covers it.
SBM-07.Cyberattack: A criminal break-in to computer systems that can steal customer data, lock files for ransom or shut down operations.
SBM-07.Changing customer tastes: Customers stop wanting what the business sells because fashions and preferences shift, leaving it with falling sales and unsold stock.
SBM-07.Equipment breakdown: Failure of a machine, computer system or power supply that the business depends on, stopping work and costing money to repair.
SBM-07.Supplier failure: A supplier delivers late, runs short or goes out of business, leaving the firm without the goods or materials it needs to sell.
SBM-07.Pandemic: A widespread outbreak of disease that can keep customers and staff away, force closures and disrupt supplies.
SBM-07.Employee errors: Mistakes or carelessness by staff, such as wrong orders or damaged goods, that cost money or lose customers.
SBM-07.Rising costs: Increases in the price of rent, supplies, wages or energy that shrink profit if they cannot be passed on to customers.
SBM-07.Cash flow shortage: Not having enough cash on hand to pay bills when they are due, even though sales may look healthy.
SBM-07.Vandalism: Deliberate damage to the property of the business, such as broken windows or graffiti, which must be paid to repair.
SBM-07.Customer nonpayment: Customers who bought on credit or paid with a bad check fail to pay, so the business loses the money it is owed.
SBM-07.New regulations: Changes in laws or taxes that raise costs, require new equipment or limit what the business may sell.
SBM-07.Product recall: Having to take back a product that turns out to be unsafe or defective, with the cost of refunds, replacements and possible injury claims.
SBM-07.Reputation damage: Loss of customers' trust through bad reviews, negative publicity or a scandal, which reduces sales.
SBM-07.Employee turnover: Workers leaving and having to be replaced, which costs money for hiring and training and can hurt service in the meantime.
SBM-07.Loss of a major customer: A customer responsible for a large share of sales stops buying, causing a sudden drop in revenue.
SBM-07.Business interruption: Being unable to operate for a time, for example after a fire or flood, so income stops while many expenses continue.
SBM-07.Technological change: New technology makes the firm's products, equipment or methods outdated, so customers move to newer alternatives.
SBM-07.Loss of a key person: The death, illness or departure of someone the business depends on, such as the founder or top salesperson. Key person insurance covers this.
SBM-07.Currency fluctuations: Changes in exchange rates that make imported supplies more expensive or reduce the value of sales made in foreign currencies.
SBM-07.Intellectual property theft: Others copying the firm's inventions, designs, brand or trade secrets without permission, taking sales that should be its own.

SBM-05.Rent: The regular payment for the space the business occupies. It is a fixed cost, due every month whatever the sales.
SBM-05.Utilities: Bills for electricity, gas, water and heating used on the premises.
SBM-05.Payroll: Wages and salaries paid to employees, usually one of the largest ongoing costs of a business.
SBM-05.Insurance: Regular premiums for policies that protect the business against losses such as fire, theft and liability claims.
SBM-05.Advertising: Money spent on promoting the business to customers, such as online ads, flyers and social media campaigns.
SBM-05.Inventory purchases: The continuing cost of restocking the goods or materials the business sells. Accountants report it as cost of goods sold, apart from other operating expenses.
SBM-05.Supplies: Items used up in running the business and not resold, such as paper, printer ink, bags and cleaning products.
SBM-05.Internet and phone: Monthly charges for internet service and telephone lines, needed to take orders and stay in touch with customers.
SBM-05.Maintenance and repairs: The cost of keeping the building and equipment in working order and fixing them when they break.
SBM-05.Software subscriptions: Recurring fees for programs and online services the business uses, such as accounting software and website hosting.
SBM-05.Shipping: The cost of sending products to customers, including postage, freight and packaging.
SBM-05.Employee benefits: Extras provided to employees on top of wages, such as health insurance, paid leave and retirement contributions.
SBM-05.Professional fees: Payments to outside experts such as accountants, bookkeepers and lawyers for their services.
SBM-05.Property taxes: Taxes charged by local government on the land, buildings and sometimes equipment that the business owns.
SBM-05.Payroll taxes: Taxes an employer pays on its workers' wages, including its share of Social Security and Medicare and unemployment taxes.
SBM-05.Loan payments: Regular payments on money the business has borrowed. Strictly, only the interest part counts as an expense, while the rest repays the debt.
SBM-05.Equipment leases: Regular payments for equipment the business rents instead of owning, such as a copier or a delivery van.
SBM-05.Cleaning: The cost of keeping the premises clean, whether through a janitorial service or cleaning staff and materials.
SBM-05.Bank and card processing fees: Charges from banks and payment companies, including the small percentage taken from every credit or debit card sale.
SBM-05.License renewals: Fees paid, often yearly, to keep business licenses and permits valid.
SBM-05.Vehicle expenses: The cost of running business vehicles and traveling for work, such as fuel, maintenance and mileage.
SBM-05.Employee training: The continuing cost of teaching staff new skills and training new hires.
SBM-05.Franchise royalties: A regular payment a franchisee makes to the franchisor, usually a percentage of sales, for continued use of the brand and system.
SBM-05.Security: Ongoing charges for protecting the premises, such as alarm monitoring or security guards.
SBM-05.Depreciation: The cost of a long-lasting asset such as equipment, spread over the years it is used. It is recorded as an expense though no cash is paid out then.
SBM-05.Dues and subscriptions: Membership fees for groups such as a trade association or chamber of commerce, and the cost of business publications.
SBM-05.Waste removal: Fees for collecting and disposing of the trash and recycling the business produces.
SBM-05.Bad debt expense: The amount customers owe that the business does not expect to collect, recorded as a cost of selling on credit.

SBM-06.Payroll: Calculating wages, withholding taxes and issuing paychecks. Specialist payroll companies do this accurately for a small fee.
SBM-06.Accounting: Keeping the financial records, preparing statements and filing tax returns, often handed to an outside accountant or bookkeeper.
SBM-06.IT support: Information technology (IT) work: setting up and fixing computers, networks and security, done by an outside technician or firm.
SBM-06.Marketing: Planning and running advertising, social media and public relations, often given to an agency or freelance specialist.
SBM-06.Web design: Building and maintaining the company website or app, usually by a freelance designer or web development firm.
SBM-06.Legal services: Advice on contracts, disputes and regulations from an outside lawyer, since few small firms can afford a lawyer on staff.
SBM-06.Customer service: Answering customers' calls, emails and chats, which can be handled by an outside call center or answering service.
SBM-06.Human resources: Recruiting, hiring paperwork and personnel policies, which an outside human resources (HR) firm can manage.
SBM-06.Cleaning: Keeping the premises clean, typically by hiring a janitorial company instead of employing cleaning staff.
SBM-06.Delivery: Storing, packing and transporting products to customers, done by courier, shipping or fulfillment companies.
SBM-06.Manufacturing: Making the product. Many small firms design and sell a product but pay a contract manufacturer to produce it.
SBM-06.Graphic design: Creating logos, packaging, ads and other visual materials, usually bought from a freelance designer when needed.
SBM-06.Maintenance and repairs: Servicing and fixing the building and equipment, done by outside tradespeople and service companies.
SBM-06.Security: Guarding the premises and monitoring alarms and cameras, provided by a security company.
SBM-06.Data entry: Typing information into computer systems and other routine office tasks, often given to a virtual assistant.
SBM-06.Payment processing: Handling customers' card and online payments, which a merchant services company does for a fee on each transaction.
SBM-06.Photography and video: Producing professional photos and videos of products, premises or staff for marketing use.
SBM-06.Printing: Producing business cards, flyers, signs and packaging, done by a print shop with equipment a small firm would not own.
SBM-06.Market research: Studying customers and competitors through surveys and data, done by a research firm with the tools and expertise.
SBM-06.Sales: Finding and selling to customers, which can be given to independent sales agents or telemarketing firms paid by commission.
SBM-06.Landscaping: Looking after the grounds outside the premises, including lawn care and snow removal.
SBM-06.Benefits administration: Managing employee benefits such as health insurance and retirement plans, including enrollment and record keeping.
SBM-06.Employee training: Teaching staff new skills, delivered by outside trainers or online courses instead of an in-house training team.
SBM-06.Writing and translation: Producing website text, ads and other written material, or converting it into other languages, usually by freelancers.
SBM-06.Debt collection: Recovering money from customers whose bills are long overdue, handed to a collection agency that keeps a share of what it recovers.

SBM-08.Write a job description: Set out the duties of the job and the skills it needs, then advertise it so suitable people can apply.
SBM-08.Interview candidates: Meet the applicants and ask about their experience and skills to judge who best fits the job.
SBM-08.Set up payroll: Put a system in place, often software or a payroll service, to calculate pay, withhold taxes and pay the employee on time.
SBM-08.Check references: Contact past employers and run any background checks allowed by law to confirm what the applicant has said.
SBM-08.Review applications: Read the resumes and application forms received and pick out the applicants worth interviewing.
SBM-08.Decide the pay: Set the wage or salary for the job, at or above the legal minimum and in line with what similar jobs pay.
SBM-08.Get an EIN: Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the Internal Revenue Service. A business needs this federal tax ID before it can pay employees.
SBM-08.Collect Form W-4: Have the new employee fill in the Internal Revenue Service form that tells the employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
SBM-08.Withhold payroll taxes: Take income tax and the employee's Social Security and Medicare taxes out of each paycheck and send them to the government.
SBM-08.Train the employee: Show the new hire how to do the job and explain the rules and routines of the business, a process often called onboarding.
SBM-08.Complete Form I-9: Fill in the federal form, checking the new hire's documents, that verifies their identity and their right to work in the United States.
SBM-08.Buy workers compensation insurance: Take out the insurance that covers medical bills and lost wages if an employee is hurt at work, as most states require of employers.
SBM-08.Make a job offer: Formally offer the position to the chosen candidate, usually in a letter stating the pay, hours and start date.
SBM-08.Budget for the hire: Work out the full cost of an employee, including wages, taxes, insurance and equipment, and confirm the business can afford it.
SBM-08.Register for unemployment insurance tax: Sign up with the state as an employer in order to pay the tax that funds benefits for workers who lose their jobs.
SBM-08.Report the new hire to the state: Send the new employee's details to the state's new hire registry shortly after hiring. States use the reports to enforce child support orders.
SBM-08.Display labor law posters: Put up the official notices about workers' rights, such as minimum wage and safety rules, where employees can see them.
SBM-08.Set up benefits: Decide which extras to offer beyond wages, such as health insurance, paid time off or a retirement plan, and arrange them.
SBM-08.Learn labor laws: Find out the rules an employer must follow, such as minimum wage, overtime, anti-discrimination and workplace safety laws.
SBM-08.Write an employee handbook: Put the workplace rules and policies in writing, covering matters such as hours, conduct, leave and discipline.
SBM-08.Set up employee records: Create a file for the employee and keep the pay, tax and personnel records the law requires employers to hold.
SBM-08.Classify the worker: Decide correctly whether the person is an employee or an independent contractor, and whether overtime pay rules apply to them.
SBM-08.File payroll tax returns: Report the wages paid and taxes withheld to the government on schedule, for example on the quarterly federal Form 941.

INO-01.Brainstorming: A group calls out as many ideas as possible on a topic, with no criticism allowed during the session. The ideas are judged only afterwards.
INO-01.Mind mapping: Drawing a diagram with the main topic in the center and related ideas branching out from it, to see connections and spark more ideas.
INO-01.Surveys: Asking many people the same set of questions about their needs and habits, to discover problems or wants a new product could address.
INO-01.Focus groups: A moderator leads a small group of consumers in an open discussion about a product area, and their comments suggest new ideas.
INO-01.Design thinking: A problem-solving approach that starts by understanding users closely, then defines their problem, generates ideas, builds prototypes and tests them.
INO-01.SCAMPER: A checklist of seven prompts for changing an existing product: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate and Reverse.
INO-01.Observation: Watching how people actually use products and go about their day, to notice difficulties they might never mention when asked.
INO-01.Customer interviews: One-to-one conversations with customers about their experiences and frustrations, which reveal needs in their own words.
INO-01.Trend analysis: Studying changes in society, technology and buying habits to predict what customers will want next.
INO-01.Competitor analysis: Examining what rival businesses offer and where they fall short, in order to find a gap or a way to do better.
INO-01.Brainwriting: A silent form of brainstorming in which people write ideas down and pass them on for others to build upon. In the 6-3-5 method, six people each write three ideas every five minutes.
INO-01.Reverse brainstorming: Asking how to cause a problem or make a product worse, then turning those answers around to find improvements.
INO-01.Free association: Writing down a word or phrase linked to the problem, then whatever it brings to mind, building a chain of thoughts that can lead to a new idea.
INO-01.Six thinking hats: Edward de Bono's method in which a group looks at an idea from six set viewpoints in turn, such as facts, feelings, risks, benefits and creativity.
INO-01.Storyboarding: Laying out a customer's experience step by step as a series of pictures or notes, which shows where a new product or improvement is needed.
INO-01.Lateral thinking: Edward de Bono's term for solving problems by approaching them from unexpected angles instead of following step-by-step logic.
INO-01.Role playing: Acting out the part of a customer or other person in a situation, to feel the problems they face and think of solutions.
INO-01.Nominal group technique: A structured meeting in which people first write ideas silently, then share them one at a time, and finally vote privately to rank them.
INO-01.Crowdsourcing: Inviting a large number of people outside the firm, usually online, to submit ideas or solutions, for example through an idea contest.
INO-01.Five whys: Asking "why?" about a problem again and again, about five times, to dig down to its root cause, which then points to what to fix.
INO-01.Gap analysis: Comparing what customers want with what is currently on offer, to find a need that no existing product meets.
INO-01.Idea journal: A notebook or file in which a person regularly writes down ideas, observations and problems as they occur, to review later.
INO-01.What-if questions: Posing imaginative questions such as "what if this cost half as much?" to break assumptions and open up new possibilities.
INO-01.Problem inventory analysis: Consumers are given a list of common problems in a product category and asked which products have them. The answers point to new product ideas.
INO-01.Attribute listing: Listing all the features of an existing product, then examining each one to see how it could be changed or improved.
INO-01.Forced relationships: Deliberately linking two unrelated products or ideas and asking what new product the combination could suggest.
INO-01.Checklist method: Working through a prepared list of questions or suggestions, such as "make it bigger?" or "other uses?", to prompt new ideas.
INO-01.Gordon method: A group technique in which members are not told the exact problem at first. They discuss a general concept, so their ideas are not narrowed too soon.
INO-01.Synectics: A group creativity method that uses analogies and metaphors to connect apparently unrelated things and see a problem in a new way.
INO-01.Collective notebook method: Each member of a group records ideas about a problem in a notebook over several weeks. A coordinator then summarizes them for group discussion.
INO-01.Morphological analysis: Breaking a product into its main dimensions, listing the options for each, and then trying new combinations of those options.
INO-01.Big-dream approach: Imagining the ideal solution with no limits on money or resources, then working back to see what part of it could be done.
INO-01.Delphi method: Experts answer questionnaires separately and anonymously over several rounds, seeing a summary of the group's views each time, until they move toward agreement.
INO-01.Parameter analysis: A two-step method: first identify the key factors (parameters) behind a need, then creatively combine them into a solution.
INO-01.Value analysis: Examining each part or function of a product and asking whether it could be done at lower cost without losing value to the customer.
INO-01.Starbursting: Generating questions about an idea instead of answers, using the six prompts who, what, where, when, why and how.

INO-02.Minimum viable product: The simplest version of a product that can be put in front of real customers to learn what they think, with the least time and money spent.
INO-02.Pivot: A deliberate change of direction in the product, the customer or the business model, made when testing shows the current plan is not working.
INO-02.Build-measure-learn: The core loop of lean startup: build a small version of the idea, measure how customers respond, learn from the results, then repeat.
INO-02.Product-market fit: The point at which a product clearly satisfies strong demand in a market: customers want it, buy it and keep using it.
INO-02.Validated learning: Knowledge about what customers really want that is backed by evidence from experiments, not by opinion or guesswork.
INO-02.Hypothesis testing: Treating each belief about the business as a guess to be checked, by running a small experiment with real customers.
INO-02.Iteration: Improving the product in repeated short cycles, changing it a little each time in response to what customers say and do.
INO-02.Customer discovery: The first step of customer development: going out to talk with potential customers to check that they really have the problem.
INO-02.Customer development: Steve Blank's process for finding and proving a market by testing ideas with customers, alongside developing the product. Lean startup grew out of it.
INO-02.A/B testing: Showing two versions of something, such as a web page, to different groups of customers at the same time to see which performs better.
INO-02.Early adopters: The first customers willing to try a new and unfinished product, because they feel the problem most keenly. Their feedback shapes it.
INO-02.Eliminating waste: Avoiding any effort that does not help the startup learn what customers want, such as building features nobody has asked for.
INO-02.Fail fast: Finding out quickly and cheaply that an idea does not work, so little is lost and the team can move on to a better one.
INO-02.Lean canvas: Ash Maurya's one-page plan for a startup, adapted from the Business Model Canvas, with boxes such as problem, solution, key metrics and unfair advantage.
INO-02.Persevere: The decision to stay on the present course because the evidence shows the plan is working. It is the alternative to a pivot.
INO-02.Vanity metrics: Numbers that look impressive, such as total downloads, but do not show whether the business is really succeeding or what to do next.
INO-02.Actionable metrics: Measurements that show clear cause and effect, so the team can tell which of its actions produced a result and decide what to do.
INO-02.Business model canvas: A one-page chart describing a business model in nine blocks, such as customer segments and revenue streams, used to sketch and test ideas.
INO-02.Continuous deployment: Releasing small updates to a product very frequently, even many times a day, so changes reach customers and get feedback quickly.
INO-02.Innovation accounting: A way of measuring a startup's progress by what it has learned and by improvements in key customer measures, instead of by early revenue.
INO-02.Leap-of-faith assumptions: The riskiest beliefs a business plan depends on, which must be tested first. The main two are that customers will value the product and that it can grow.
INO-02.Small batches: Doing work in small amounts and finishing each quickly, so problems are found early and less effort is wasted.
INO-02.Engines of growth: Eric Ries's three ways a startup grows steadily: sticky (keeping customers), viral (customers bring in others) and paid (buying customers with advertising).
INO-02.Five whys: Asking "why?" about five times when something goes wrong, to trace the problem to its root cause instead of fixing only the symptom.
INO-02.Cohort analysis: Comparing groups of customers who joined at different times, to see whether newer groups behave better than older ones as the product changes.
INO-02.Concierge MVP: A test in which the founders deliver the service by hand to a few customers, and the customers know it, before building any technology.
INO-02.Smoke test: Offering a product that does not exist yet, for example on a web page with a sign-up button, to measure how many people show interest.

INO-03.Product innovation: Creating a new good or significantly improving an existing one, such as the first smartphone.
INO-03.Process innovation: A new or better way of making or delivering a product, such as the assembly line, which lowers cost or raises quality.
INO-03.Disruptive innovation: Clayton Christensen's term for a simpler, cheaper offering that starts with overlooked customers and gradually takes over the market from established firms.
INO-03.Incremental innovation: A series of small improvements to an existing product or process, such as each year's slightly better phone model.
INO-03.Radical innovation: A breakthrough that is completely new and changes how people live or how an industry works, such as the airplane or the internet.
INO-03.Technological innovation: Innovation that comes from new scientific or technical knowledge, in the form of new devices, materials or methods.
INO-03.Service innovation: A new or improved service, or a new way of delivering one, such as online banking or ride-hailing.
INO-03.Business model innovation: A new way of creating and capturing value, changing how a firm makes money instead of what it sells, such as streaming by subscription.
INO-03.Sustaining innovation: Christensen's term for improvements that make existing products better for a firm's current customers, keeping it competitive.
INO-03.Marketing innovation: A new method of marketing, involving significant changes in a product's packaging, placement, promotion or pricing.
INO-03.Digital innovation: Using digital technology, such as software, apps and data, to create new products or change how a business operates.
INO-03.Organizational innovation: A new way of organizing a business, such as a new management structure, workplace practice or way of working with partners.
INO-03.Open innovation: Henry Chesbrough's term for developing new products by using ideas from outside the firm, such as customers, universities and partners, as well as inside.
INO-03.Social innovation: A new solution to a social problem, such as poverty or poor health, where the main benefit goes to society and not to private owners.
INO-03.Green innovation: New products or processes that reduce harm to the environment, for example by saving energy or cutting waste and pollution.
INO-03.Market-creating innovation: An innovation that makes a product simple and affordable enough to reach people who could not buy it before, creating a new market.
INO-03.Architectural innovation: Rearranging existing components and technologies into a new design or system, without changing the components themselves.
INO-03.Frugal innovation: Redesigning a product to strip out costly extras so it does the essential job at a much lower price for customers with little money.
INO-03.Reverse innovation: An innovation first developed for emerging markets, usually simple and low-cost, that is later sold in wealthy countries as well.
INO-03.Closed innovation: The traditional approach in which a firm develops new ideas entirely with its own staff and keeps them secret. It is the opposite of open innovation.
INO-03.Modular innovation: Replacing one component of a product with a new technology while the overall design stays the same, such as a digital dial in place of an analog one.
INO-03.Dynamically continuous innovation: A noticeably new version of an existing product that requires some change in how people use it, but not totally new habits.
INO-03.Efficiency innovation: Christensen's term for innovation that lets a firm make the same product with fewer resources, lowering costs and freeing up capital.
INO-03.Channel innovation: A new way of getting a product to customers, such as selling directly online instead of through shops.
INO-03.Brand innovation: A fresh way of presenting what a business stands for, through a new brand or a new use of an existing one, that makes its offer distinctive.

INO-04.Survey: A set of questions put to many potential customers, on paper or online, to learn whether they want the product and what they would pay.
INO-04.Prototype: A working model or mock-up of the product that customers can see and try, so their reactions can guide changes before production.
INO-04.Focus group: A small group of target customers who discuss the idea with a moderator, giving detailed opinions on what they like and dislike.
INO-04.Customer interviews: One-to-one conversations with likely customers about their problem and the proposed solution, to check that the need is real.
INO-04.Minimum viable product: The most basic version of the product that still works, released to early customers to see how they respond before more is built.
INO-04.Crowdfunding campaign: Presenting the idea on a platform such as Kickstarter and asking the public to back it. Strong backing is evidence that people want it.
INO-04.Pre-orders: Inviting customers to order and pay before the product is made. People committing real money is strong proof of demand.
INO-04.Social media feedback: Posting the idea, pictures or a poll on social platforms and judging interest from the comments, shares and votes.
INO-04.Test market: Selling the product in one limited area or to a small group first, to see how it performs before a full launch.
INO-04.Beta test: Giving a nearly finished product to a limited group of outside users, who try it in real conditions and report problems.
INO-04.Pop-up shop: A temporary stall or store, for example at a farmers market or fair, used to sell the product face to face and watch how customers react.
INO-04.Free samples: Giving people the product, or a trial of the service, at no charge and collecting their reactions.
INO-04.Landing page: A simple web page that describes the product and asks visitors to sign up or join a waiting list, used to measure interest.
INO-04.Sell a small batch: Making and selling a limited quantity first, to see whether it sells and what buyers say, before investing in large production.
INO-04.Ask friends and family: Getting first reactions from people you know. It is easy and cheap, though they may be too kind to give honest criticism.
INO-04.A/B testing: Showing two versions of an offer, such as two prices or web pages, to different groups to see which draws the better response.
INO-04.Online ad test: Running small, cheap internet ads for the idea and counting how many people click, to gauge interest before building it.
INO-04.Concept test: Describing the idea to target customers in words or pictures, before any product exists, and asking how likely they would be to buy.
INO-04.Usability testing: Watching real users try to use the product or a prototype, to find out where they get confused or stuck.
INO-04.Trade show: Displaying the product at an industry exhibition to collect reactions and orders from buyers and others in the trade.
INO-04.Concierge test: The founder delivers the service personally and by hand to a few customers, to learn what they value before building any system.
INO-04.Wizard of Oz test: Customers use what looks like a finished automated product, while people secretly do the work behind the scenes to test demand.
INO-04.Smoke test: Advertising a product that has not been built, for example with a "buy" or "sign up" button, to count how many people try to get it.
INO-04.Letter of intent: A signed written statement from a customer, usually a business, that it intends to buy the product once it is available.
INO-04.Explainer video: A short video showing how the product would work, released before it is built to see how many viewers sign up or ask for it.

INO-05.Lower price: Charging less than rivals for a similar product, which requires keeping the business's own costs lower. The strategy is called cost leadership.
INO-05.Better quality: Offering a product that performs better, lasts longer or is more reliable than competitors' versions.
INO-05.Customer service: Treating customers better than rivals do, with helpful staff, quick answers and personal attention.
INO-05.Unique product: Offering something with features or a design that customers cannot get elsewhere. The strategy is called differentiation.
INO-05.Convenience: Making it easier to buy, through a handy location, longer opening hours, online ordering or a simpler process.
INO-05.Brand: A name and reputation that customers recognize and trust, which makes them choose the business and stay loyal to it.
INO-05.Speed: Serving customers or delivering orders faster than competitors do.
INO-05.Patent: A government grant giving an inventor the sole right to make and sell an invention for a limited time, about 20 years, which keeps rivals from copying it.
INO-05.Niche focus: Concentrating on one small, specific group of customers and serving their particular needs better than general competitors can.
INO-05.Customization: Making or adapting the product to each customer's own wishes instead of selling the same thing to everyone.
INO-05.First-mover advantage: The lead gained by being first into a market, such as winning customers and recognition before rivals arrive.
INO-05.Skilled employees: Staff whose knowledge, talent and experience let the business do things competitors cannot easily match.
INO-05.Wide selection: Offering more choice of products, styles or sizes than competitors, so customers are more likely to find what they want.
INO-05.Sustainability: Running the business in an environmentally and socially responsible way, which attracts customers who care about those issues.
INO-05.Customer relationships: Close, lasting ties with customers, built by knowing them well and rewarding their loyalty, so they keep coming back.
INO-05.Trade secret: Valuable business information, such as a recipe or formula, that gives an edge because it is kept confidential. It is protected for as long as it stays secret.
INO-05.Economies of scale: The fall in cost per unit as a business produces or buys in larger quantities, which lets it charge less or earn more than smaller rivals.
INO-05.Exclusive contracts: Agreements that give the business the sole right to sell a product, use a supplier or serve an area, shutting competitors out.
INO-05.Network effects: A product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it, as with a social network, making it hard for newcomers to catch up.
INO-05.Supply chain strength: Reliable suppliers and efficient distribution that get products to customers faster, cheaper or more dependably than rivals can.
INO-05.Guarantee: A promise to refund, repair or replace if the customer is not satisfied, which lowers the buyer's risk and builds trust.
INO-05.Agility: The ability to respond quickly to changes in customer wants or market conditions. Small businesses can often move faster than large ones.
INO-05.Local focus: Being part of the community: locally owned, knowing local customers and tastes, and using local suppliers.
INO-05.Operational efficiency: Running the business with less waste of time, materials and money than competitors, which keeps costs down.
INO-05.Switching costs: The time, money or effort a customer would have to spend to change to a competitor. The higher these are, the more customers stay.
INO-05.Company culture: The shared values and ways of working inside a business. A strong culture motivates staff and is very hard for rivals to copy.
INO-05.Access to scarce resources: Control of something competitors cannot easily obtain, such as a prime location, a rare material or a limited license.
INO-05.Proprietary data: Information the business has gathered that no one else has, such as customer data, which it can use to serve customers better.

INO-06.Artificial intelligence: Computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human thinking, such as understanding language, recognizing images and writing text.
INO-06.Mobile apps: Software programs for smartphones and tablets, which let businesses sell to and serve customers wherever they are.
INO-06.Virtual and augmented reality: Virtual reality places the user inside a computer-made world through a headset. Augmented reality adds digital images on top of the real world.
INO-06.Robotics: Machines that carry out physical tasks automatically, such as assembling products, moving goods in warehouses or cleaning.
INO-06.Electric vehicles: Cars and trucks powered by batteries instead of gasoline or diesel, creating openings in charging, batteries, servicing and software.
INO-06.Social media and e-commerce: Online platforms for sharing content and for buying and selling, which let even a tiny business reach and sell to customers anywhere.
INO-06.3D printing: Building a solid object layer by layer from a digital design, also called additive manufacturing. It makes small production runs affordable.
INO-06.Drones: Small pilotless aircraft flown by remote control or computer, used for photography, inspections, farming and deliveries.
INO-06.Cloud computing: Renting computing power, storage and software over the internet instead of buying and running your own servers.
INO-06.Blockchain: A shared digital record of transactions kept on many computers at once, which is very hard to alter. It is the technology behind cryptocurrencies.
INO-06.Autonomous vehicles: Cars, trucks and other vehicles that use sensors and software to drive themselves with little or no human control.
INO-06.Internet of Things: Everyday objects such as thermostats, appliances and machines fitted with sensors and connected to the internet so they can send and receive data.
INO-06.Renewable energy: Power from sources that are naturally replaced, such as sunlight and wind, creating business in installation, equipment and services.
INO-06.Big data: Extremely large sets of information that businesses analyze with special tools to find patterns and make better decisions.
INO-06.5G: The fifth generation of mobile network technology, with much faster speeds and quicker response than 4G, supporting many more connected devices.
INO-06.Fintech: Short for financial technology: using software and apps to deliver financial services such as payments, lending and investing.
INO-06.Remote work technology: Tools such as video meetings and shared online workspaces that let people work together from different places.
INO-06.Wearable technology: Electronic devices worn on the body, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers, that collect data and connect to a phone.
INO-06.Biotechnology: Using living cells and biological processes to make products such as medicines, improved crops and new materials.
INO-06.Telehealth: Providing health care at a distance, for example a doctor's appointment by video call or remote monitoring of patients.
INO-06.Voice assistants: Software that understands spoken commands and answers aloud, found in phones and smart speakers.
INO-06.Cybersecurity: Tools and services that protect computers, networks and data from attack. Rising online crime keeps demand growing.
INO-06.Battery storage: Improved batteries that store more electricity for less money, important for electric vehicles and for saving solar and wind power.
INO-06.Quantum computing: A new kind of computer that uses the principles of quantum physics and may solve certain problems far faster than ordinary computers.
INO-06.Nanotechnology: Engineering materials and devices at the scale of atoms and molecules, giving them new properties for medicine, electronics and coatings.
INO-06.Biometrics: Identifying people by physical traits such as fingerprints, faces or voices, used for security and for fast log-ins and payments.
INO-06.Edge computing: Processing data close to where it is created, on local devices, instead of sending it all to distant data centers. This gives faster responses.
INO-06.Space technology: Commercial rockets, satellites and related services, such as satellite internet, made far cheaper by reusable launch vehicles.
INO-06.Alternative proteins: Foods that replace conventional meat and dairy, made from plants, by fermentation or by growing animal cells.
INO-06.Digital twins: Detailed virtual copies of real objects or systems, fed with live data, used to test changes and predict problems without touching the real thing.
INO-06.Hydrogen fuel cells: Devices that produce electricity by combining hydrogen with oxygen, giving off only water. They can power vehicles and buildings.
INO-06.Carbon capture: Technology that traps carbon dioxide from factories or from the air and stores or reuses it, so it does not add to climate change.
INO-06.No-code tools: Software that lets people build apps and websites by dragging and dropping visual blocks, without writing programming code.

INO-07.Solves a problem: The idea meets a real need or removes a real difficulty that customers have. Without that, there is no reason for anyone to buy.
INO-07.Market demand: Enough people want the product and are willing and able to pay for it to support a business.
INO-07.Profitable: The product can be sold for more than it costs to make and deliver, leaving a profit for the owner.
INO-07.Feasible: The idea can actually be carried out with the technology, skills and money that are realistically available.
INO-07.Unique: The idea differs from what is already on offer in a way customers value, giving them a reason to choose it.
INO-07.Limited competition: Few rivals already serve the need well, so a new business has room to win customers.
INO-07.Affordable to start: The money needed to launch is within what the founder can realistically raise.
INO-07.Competitive advantage: The business would have an edge that rivals cannot easily copy, such as a patent or special skill, so it can keep its customers.
INO-07.Good timing: The market is ready for the idea now. The period during which a new business can successfully enter is called the window of opportunity.
INO-07.Fit with founder skills: The idea matches the founder's own skills, experience, interests and goals, making it more likely to be carried out well.
INO-07.Resources available: The money, people, materials and equipment that the business needs can actually be obtained.
INO-07.Scalable: The business can grow to serve many more customers without its costs rising just as fast.
INO-07.Legal: The product and the way it is sold are permitted by law and can meet the regulations that apply.
INO-07.Adds value: Customers gain a benefit worth more to them than the price they pay, such as saving time, money or effort.
INO-07.Attractive: The idea appeals to customers, and the likely returns make it worth the effort for the founder and investors. One of the standard marks of an opportunity.
INO-07.Manageable risk: The dangers involved are understood and are small enough, or controllable enough, to be worth taking for the expected reward.
INO-07.Tested with customers: Real potential customers have tried or seen the idea and shown that they want it, so demand is proven instead of assumed.
INO-07.Durable: Demand will last long enough for the business to recover its investment and earn a profit. It is not a passing fad.
INO-07.Repeat customers: Buyers will come back and purchase again and again, giving steady sales instead of a single sale each.

FRN-01.Initial franchise fee: A one-time payment to the franchisor when the agreement is signed, for the right to open an outlet under its brand and system.
FRN-01.Royalties: Ongoing payments to the franchisor, usually a percentage of the outlet's sales, due every week or month for the life of the agreement.
FRN-01.Advertising fee: A regular contribution, often a percentage of sales, to a fund the franchisor uses for national or regional advertising of the brand.
FRN-01.Equipment: The machines and fixtures the franchisor's system requires, such as ovens, fryers or cash registers, which the franchisee must buy or lease.
FRN-01.Inventory: The opening stock of products and supplies needed to start trading, and the cost of restocking them afterwards.
FRN-01.Rent: The cost of leasing the premises. The franchisee, not the franchisor, normally pays for the location.
FRN-01.Payroll: Wages for the outlet's staff. They are the franchisee's employees, so the franchisee pays them.
FRN-01.Build-out costs: The cost of constructing or remodeling the premises to the franchisor's required design and layout.
FRN-01.Insurance: Premiums for the insurance policies the franchise agreement requires the franchisee to carry, such as liability and property coverage.
FRN-01.Training fee: A charge for the franchisor's training program, or the travel and living costs of attending it when the training itself is included.
FRN-01.Licenses and permits: Government fees for the business license and any permits the outlet needs, such as health or signage permits.
FRN-01.Utilities: The outlet's bills for electricity, gas, water and similar services, including any deposits to start them.
FRN-01.Technology fee: A regular charge for using the franchisor's required software, such as the point-of-sale and ordering systems.
FRN-01.Signage: The cost of the signs that display the brand, which must be made to the franchisor's exact specifications.
FRN-01.Grand opening costs: Money the franchisee must spend on advertising and events to launch the new outlet. Many agreements set a minimum amount.
FRN-01.Working capital: Cash the franchisee needs on hand to cover running costs in the first months, before the outlet earns enough to pay its own way.
FRN-01.Renewal fee: A fee paid to the franchisor to extend the franchise agreement for a further term when the first term ends.
FRN-01.Legal and accounting fees: Payments to a lawyer to review the franchise documents and to an accountant to check the figures and set up the books.
FRN-01.Required purchases from the franchisor: Products, ingredients or supplies that the agreement obliges the franchisee to buy from the franchisor or its approved suppliers.
FRN-01.Taxes: The outlet's own business taxes, such as income, property and payroll taxes, which the franchisee must pay like any other owner.
FRN-01.Transfer fee: A fee charged by the franchisor when a franchisee sells the outlet and the agreement passes to a new owner.
FRN-01.Audit fee: The cost of the franchisor's inspection of the franchisee's books, usually charged to the franchisee if it shows sales were under-reported.
FRN-01.Late fees: Penalties or interest charged by the franchisor when royalties or other payments are not made on time.
FRN-01.Area development fee: A fee paid for the right to open several outlets in a defined territory over an agreed period.
FRN-01.Uniforms: The branded clothing the franchisor requires staff to wear, which the franchisee must supply.

FRN-02.Brand recognition: Customers already know and trust the franchise name, so a new outlet attracts buyers from the day it opens.
FRN-02.Training: The franchisor teaches the new owner how to run the business, from making the product to managing staff and accounts.
FRN-02.Ongoing support: The franchisor keeps giving help and advice after opening, for example through field visits, a help line and updates to the system.
FRN-02.Proven business model: The way of running the business has already been tested and shown to work in other outlets, so the franchisee is not experimenting.
FRN-02.Lower risk: Because the brand and system are already tested, a franchise is generally thought less likely to fail than a brand-new independent business.
FRN-02.National advertising: The franchisor runs large advertising campaigns, paid for from all the outlets' pooled fees, that a single small business could never afford.
FRN-02.Existing customer base: People who already buy from the brand elsewhere will come to a new outlet without having to be won over.
FRN-02.Proven products: The goods or menu items have already been developed and shown to sell, so the franchisee does not have to invent them.
FRN-02.Being your own boss: The franchisee owns and runs the outlet and keeps its profits, while still following the franchisor's rules.
FRN-02.Easier financing: Lenders are more willing to lend for a franchise with a known record, and some franchisors offer or arrange financing themselves.
FRN-02.Buying power: The franchise chain buys supplies in huge quantities for all its outlets, getting lower prices than a lone business could.
FRN-02.Standardized operations: The franchisor supplies set procedures, usually in an operations manual, covering every task, so quality is consistent and nothing has to be worked out from scratch.
FRN-02.Established suppliers: The franchisor has already found and approved reliable suppliers, so the franchisee does not have to search for them.
FRN-02.Less experience needed: Because the system and training are supplied, a person can run a franchise without previous experience in that industry.
FRN-02.Site selection help: The franchisor uses its experience and data to help the franchisee choose a location likely to succeed.
FRN-02.Exclusive territory: An area in which the franchisor agrees not to open or license another outlet, protecting the franchisee from competition within the brand.
FRN-02.Faster startup: With the design, suppliers and procedures already worked out, a franchise can open and start earning sooner than a business built from nothing.
FRN-02.Technology and systems: The franchisee gets the use of software already developed for the chain, such as ordering, checkout and stock control systems.
FRN-02.Use of trademarks: The legal right to trade under the franchisor's protected name, logo and other brand symbols.
FRN-02.Network of franchisees: Other owners in the same chain, who can share advice and experience because they run the same business elsewhere.
FRN-02.Research and development: The franchisor pays for developing and testing new products and methods, and passes the results on to every outlet.
FRN-02.Easier resale: An outlet of a well-known brand is usually easier to sell to a new owner, and may fetch a better price, than an unknown independent business.

FRN-03.High startup cost: The franchise fee comes on top of the usual costs of opening a business, so the total investment is often very large.
FRN-03.Royalties: A percentage of sales must be paid to the franchisor continually, whether or not the outlet is making a profit.
FRN-03.Less control: The franchisor makes many of the big decisions, so the owner has much less independence than in a business of their own design.
FRN-03.Strict rules: The franchisee must follow the franchisor's detailed standards on everything from recipes to uniforms, with little room for their own ideas.
FRN-03.Shared reputation: Every outlet carries the same name, so bad service or a scandal at one outlet or at head office can drive customers away from all of them.
FRN-03.Advertising fees: The franchisee must pay into the brand's advertising fund but has little say in how the money is spent or whether it helps their own area.
FRN-03.Limited product offerings: The franchisee may sell only the products the franchisor approves and cannot add items that local customers ask for.
FRN-03.Required suppliers: Supplies must be bought from the franchisor or its approved sources, even when the same goods are cheaper elsewhere.
FRN-03.Pricing set by the franchisor: The franchisor strongly influences prices and promotions, so the franchisee may have to sell at prices that squeeze their own profit.
FRN-03.Still a risk of failure: A well-known name does not guarantee success. An outlet can still fail through a poor location, weak management or a declining brand.
FRN-03.Long-term contract: The agreement ties the franchisee in for many years, often ten or more, and leaving early is difficult and costly.
FRN-03.Territory limits: The franchisee may operate only in the area assigned, and the franchisor may be free to place other outlets close by.
FRN-03.Contract may not be renewed: When the term ends the franchisor may decline to renew, and it can end the agreement early if its rules are broken.
FRN-03.Weak franchisor support: Some franchisors give less training and help than they promised, leaving the franchisee paying fees for little in return.
FRN-03.Conflict with the franchisor: Disagreements can arise over fees, rules or new requirements, and the franchisor usually holds the stronger position under the contract.
FRN-03.Resale restrictions: The franchisee cannot sell the outlet to whomever they choose. The franchisor must approve the buyer and may charge a fee.
FRN-03.Franchisor failure: If the franchisor is badly managed or goes bankrupt, the franchisee loses the brand value and support they paid for.
FRN-03.Franchisor inspections: The franchisor checks outlets and their records regularly to make sure its standards are met and sales are reported correctly.
FRN-03.Required upgrades: The franchisor can require the franchisee to remodel the premises or buy new equipment, at the franchisee's own expense.
FRN-03.Non-compete clause: A contract term that stops the franchisee from running a similar business during the agreement and for a period after it ends.

FRN-04.Initial fees: The payments due to the franchisor before the outlet opens, chiefly the initial franchise fee, and whether any of it is refundable.
FRN-04.Estimated initial investment: A table of everything the franchisee is expected to spend to open, such as fees, equipment, rent and opening cash, given as low and high estimates.
FRN-04.Royalties and other fees: The continuing payments the franchisee must make, such as royalties, advertising contributions and charges for transfers or renewals.
FRN-04.Litigation history: Certain lawsuits and legal actions involving the franchisor and its executives, which may reveal disputes with franchisees or fraud claims.
FRN-04.Franchisor financial statements: Audited financial statements of the franchisor, which let a buyer judge whether the company is financially sound.
FRN-04.Territory: Whether the franchisee receives a protected area, and whether the franchisor can open or license competing outlets nearby.
FRN-04.Trademarks: The names, logos and symbols the franchisee will be allowed to use, and whether they are registered and legally protected.
FRN-04.Training and assistance: The help the franchisor is obliged to give, including the training program, help with opening and continuing support.
FRN-04.Bankruptcy history: Any bankruptcy in recent years involving the franchisor or its executives, a warning sign about financial stability.
FRN-04.Franchisee obligations: A summary table of the franchisee's main duties under the agreement, with references to where each appears in the contract.
FRN-04.Franchisor business experience: The work history of the franchisor's directors and senior managers, showing whether they have the experience to run the system.
FRN-04.Renewal and termination terms: The length of the agreement, how it can be renewed, when either side may end it, whether it can be sold on, and how disputes are settled.
FRN-04.The franchisor and its affiliates: Who the franchisor is, its history, and any parent or related companies, along with a description of the business being offered.
FRN-04.Advertising program: How the franchisor advertises the brand, what the franchisee must contribute and how the advertising fund is spent.
FRN-04.List of outlets: Tables showing how many outlets have opened, closed and changed hands, with contact details of current and former franchisees a buyer can call.
FRN-04.Financial performance representations: Any statements about how much an outlet sells or earns. Franchisors need not give these, but if they do, the figures must appear here with a reasonable basis.
FRN-04.Supplier restrictions: What the franchisee must buy from the franchisor or from approved suppliers, and whether the franchisor earns money on those purchases.
FRN-04.Financing: The terms of any loans or other financing the franchisor offers or arranges for franchisees.
FRN-04.Restrictions on what the franchisee may: The limits on the goods and services the franchisee may offer and on the customers they may sell to.
FRN-04.Contracts: Copies of the franchise agreement and every other contract the franchisee will be asked to sign, attached to the document.
FRN-04.Patents and copyrights: Any patents, copyrights and confidential know-how the franchisee will use, and the limits on how they may use them.
FRN-04.Public figures: Any celebrity or well-known person paid to promote the franchise, what they are paid and whether they have invested in or help manage the franchisor.
FRN-04.Obligation to participate in the busines: Whether the franchisee must personally run the outlet day to day or may hire a manager to do so.
FRN-04.Computer system requirements: The computer hardware and software the franchisee must buy and use, its cost, and the franchisor's access to the data in it.
FRN-04.Receipt: The final pages, which the buyer signs and dates to prove when the document was received. This matters because of the 14-day waiting period.

FRN-05.Liability: How far the owners are personally responsible for the debts and lawsuits of the business. Some forms put personal assets at risk and others protect them.
FRN-05.Taxes: How the profit is taxed. In some forms it is taxed once on the owners' personal returns, while a regular corporation's profit is taxed twice.
FRN-05.Cost to form: The money and effort needed to set the business up. A sole proprietorship costs almost nothing, while a corporation needs filings and fees.
FRN-05.Control: Who makes the decisions. A sole owner decides everything, while partners and shareholders must share authority.
FRN-05.Ability to raise capital: How easily the business can obtain money. Corporations can sell shares to investors, while a sole owner is limited to personal funds and loans.
FRN-05.Number of owners: How many people will own the business. One person can be a sole proprietor, but two or more need a partnership, LLC or corporation.
FRN-05.Paperwork: The amount of record keeping, reports and legal formalities the form requires. Corporations face the most and sole proprietorships the least.
FRN-05.Continuity: Whether the business carries on if an owner dies or leaves. A corporation continues, while a sole proprietorship legally ends with its owner.
FRN-05.Profit distribution: Who receives the profits and how they are divided: all to one owner, shared among partners, or paid to shareholders as dividends.
FRN-05.Type of business: The nature, size and riskiness of the activity. A risky or large business has more need of the protection of an LLC or corporation.
FRN-05.Future goals: What the owners plan for the business, such as fast growth, bringing in investors or selling it, since some forms suit those plans better.
FRN-05.Transfer of ownership: How easily an owner can sell or pass on their share. Corporate shares transfer easily, while a partner usually needs the others' consent.
FRN-05.Management expertise: The range of skills needed to run the business. A sole owner must supply them alone, while partners or a corporation can combine several people's talents.
FRN-05.Flexibility: How freely the owners can arrange management and the sharing of profits, and how easily the business can change as it develops.
FRN-05.Privacy: How much information must be made public. Corporations must disclose more, while a sole proprietor can keep finances private.
FRN-05.Ease of dissolving: How simple it is to close the business down. A sole owner can just stop, while a corporation must go through a formal legal process.
FRN-05.State laws: The rules of the state where the business is formed, since each state sets its own requirements, fees and taxes for each form of ownership.
FRN-05.Credibility: The impression the form gives. Having "Inc." or "LLC" after the name can make a business look more established to customers and lenders.

FRN-06.Financial statements: The income statements, balance sheets and tax returns for several past years, which show whether the business really earns what the seller claims.
FRN-06.Reason for selling: Why the owner wants out. Retirement is harmless, but a hidden reason such as falling sales or a new competitor is a warning.
FRN-06.Debts and liabilities: What the business owes, including loans, unpaid bills, back taxes and claims on its property, some of which could pass to the buyer.
FRN-06.Customer base: Who the customers are, how loyal they are and whether they are likely to stay after the business changes hands.
FRN-06.Reputation: What customers and the community think of the business. A good name, called goodwill, adds value, and a bad one is hard to repair.
FRN-06.Location: Whether the site still suits the business, considering traffic, the neighborhood and any changes planned for the area.
FRN-06.Condition of equipment: Whether the machinery, building and other physical assets are in good working order or will soon need costly repair or replacement.
FRN-06.Inventory: The stock included in the sale: how much there is, whether it is current and saleable, and whether it is valued fairly.
FRN-06.Asking price: What the seller wants for the business, which the buyer should compare with an independent estimate of its value.
FRN-06.Growth potential: Whether sales and profits are likely to rise in future, judged from trends in the industry and the local market.
FRN-06.Lease: The terms of the rental agreement for the premises, how long it has left, and whether it can be transferred to the new owner.
FRN-06.Competition: Who the rivals are, how strong they are, and whether new ones are about to arrive.
FRN-06.Employees: The skills and attitude of the staff, what they are paid, and whether key people will stay on under a new owner.
FRN-06.Contracts: Agreements with suppliers, customers and others, and whether they remain valid when the business is sold.
FRN-06.Pending lawsuits: Any current or threatened legal claims against the business, which could become the buyer's problem.
FRN-06.Licenses and permits: Whether the business holds the licenses, permits and zoning approval it needs, and whether they can be transferred to a new owner.
FRN-06.Intellectual property: Whether the business truly owns its patents, trademarks, brand name and trade secrets, and whether they pass to the buyer.
FRN-06.Operating procedures: How the business runs day to day, including its systems and technology, and whether they are written down so a new owner can follow them.
FRN-06.Accounts receivable: Money customers owe the business. The buyer should check how old these debts are, since long-overdue ones may never be paid.
FRN-06.Seller non-compete agreement: A promise by the seller not to open a competing business nearby for a set time, so the customers are not taken away.
FRN-06.Environmental issues: Any pollution or contamination on the property, which the new owner could be legally required to clean up.
FRN-06.Dependence on the owner: How much the success of the business rests on the current owner's personal skills and relationships, which leave when the owner does.
FRN-06.Insurance coverage: What insurance policies the business has, their cost, and its history of claims, which hints at past problems.

FRN-07.Business format franchise: The franchisee gets the whole way of doing business: the brand, products, operating methods, training and marketing. Most fast-food chains work this way.
FRN-07.Product distribution franchise: The franchisee is licensed to sell the franchisor's products under its trade name, as car dealers do, without receiving a complete operating system.
FRN-07.Single-unit franchise: The most basic arrangement: the franchisee buys the right to open and run one outlet.
FRN-07.Multi-unit franchise: One franchisee owns and operates more than one outlet of the same brand.
FRN-07.Master franchise: The master franchisee buys the rights to a large territory, often a country, and can sell franchises to others there, sharing the fees with the franchisor.
FRN-07.Area development franchise: The franchisee agrees to open a set number of outlets in a defined territory on an agreed schedule, and runs them all.
FRN-07.Manufacturing franchise: The franchisor licenses a manufacturer to make and sell products using its name and formula, as soft-drink companies do with bottlers.
FRN-07.Conversion franchise: An existing independent business joins a franchise system, taking on its brand and methods, as many real estate offices and hotels have done.
FRN-07.Co-branding: Two franchise brands operate together in one location, sharing space and customers, such as two restaurant brands under one roof.
FRN-07.Owner-operator franchise: The franchisee personally works in and manages the outlet every day instead of hiring a manager.
FRN-07.Retail franchise: A franchise that sells goods to shoppers from a store, such as a convenience store or clothing shop.
FRN-07.Job franchise: A low-cost franchise in which the owner does the work personally, often from home or a van with few or no staff, such as cleaning or repair services.
FRN-07.Investment franchise: A franchise needing a very large sum of capital, such as a hotel. The franchisee is mainly an investor and hires a management team to run it.
FRN-07.Home-based franchise: A franchise run from the owner's home with no shop or office, typically a service delivered at customers' premises or online.
FRN-07.Management franchise: The franchisee manages the business and its staff, who do the hands-on work, instead of doing that work personally.
FRN-07.Area representative franchise: The representative recruits and supports franchisees in a territory for a share of the fees, but the franchisees sign their contracts with the franchisor.
FRN-07.Absentee ownership franchise: The owner invests in the franchise but leaves the daily running to a hired manager, often while keeping another job.
FRN-07.Joint venture franchise: The franchisor and a local partner jointly own and invest in the outlets, sharing the profits and risks. It is common when entering foreign markets.
FRN-07.Manufacturer-retailer franchise: A manufacturer licenses retailers to sell its products, as car makers do with dealerships and oil companies with service stations.
FRN-07.Manufacturer-wholesaler franchise: A manufacturer licenses wholesalers to distribute its product, as soft-drink makers license bottlers who then supply retailers.
FRN-07.Wholesaler-retailer franchise: A wholesaler licenses independent retailers to trade under a common name and buy stock through it, as with some hardware and grocery groups.
FRN-07.Service sponsor-retailer franchise: A service company licenses its name and operating system to independent outlets that deliver the service, as in fast food, hotels and car rental.

FRN-08.Easy to start: The simplest form to set up. One person can begin trading with little more than any local licenses that the type of business requires.
FRN-08.Full control: The owner makes every decision alone, with no partners, shareholders or board to consult.
FRN-08.Keep all profits: Everything the business earns after expenses belongs to the single owner and does not have to be shared.
FRN-08.Low startup cost: There are few or no legal fees and filings to create the business, so it is the cheapest form to set up.
FRN-08.Taxed once: The business pays no separate income tax. Its profit is taxed only as the owner's personal income, which is called pass-through taxation.
FRN-08.Few regulations: Sole proprietorships face the least government paperwork and fewest legal formalities of any form of ownership.
FRN-08.Quick decisions: With no one else to consult, the owner can decide and act immediately when conditions change.
FRN-08.Flexibility: The owner can change products, hours or direction at will, without needing anyone's agreement.
FRN-08.Easy to dissolve: The owner can close the business simply by ceasing to trade and paying its debts, with no formal legal process.
FRN-08.Privacy: The owner does not have to publish financial reports or reveal business information to the public or to shareholders.
FRN-08.Pride of ownership: The personal satisfaction of knowing the business and its success are entirely the owner's own work.
FRN-08.Simple tax filing: Business income and expenses are reported on a form attached to the owner's personal return, Schedule C, with no separate business return.
FRN-08.Close contact with customers: The owner usually deals with customers personally, so gets to know them and can respond to their wishes directly.
FRN-08.Losses offset other income: A loss in the business can generally be deducted from the owner's other income on the personal tax return, reducing the tax owed.

GRO-01.Opening new locations: Adding more stores or branches in other places, so the business can reach customers it could not serve from one site.
GRO-01.Franchising: Letting other people open outlets under the brand and system in return for fees and royalties, so growth is paid for with their money.
GRO-01.Product development: Creating new or improved products to sell to the customers the business already has. One of the four strategies in the Ansoff matrix.
GRO-01.Mergers and acquisitions: Growing by combining with another company (a merger) or buying one (an acquisition), instead of building from within.
GRO-01.Diversification: Moving into new products and new markets at the same time. It is the riskiest of the four strategies in the Ansoff matrix.
GRO-01.Market penetration: Selling more of the existing products in the existing market, for example through more promotion or lower prices, to win market share.
GRO-01.Market development: Taking existing products into new markets, such as a new region or a new group of customers. One of the four Ansoff matrix strategies.
GRO-01.E-commerce: Selling through a website or online marketplace, which lets the business reach customers far beyond its physical location.
GRO-01.Exporting: Selling products made at home to customers in other countries, which opens up much larger markets.
GRO-01.Licensing: Allowing another company to make or sell the product, or use the brand, in return for a royalty, so growth needs little investment.
GRO-01.Strategic alliance: An agreement between two businesses to cooperate, for example by sharing distribution or technology, while each stays independent.
GRO-01.Joint venture: Two or more businesses set up and jointly own a new operation for a specific purpose, sharing its costs, risks and profits.
GRO-01.Organic growth: Growing from within, by increasing the firm's own sales and reinvesting its profits, instead of by buying other companies.
GRO-01.Increasing capacity: Adding staff, equipment or space so the business can produce more and serve more customers.
GRO-01.Improving customer retention: Keeping existing customers buying for longer, through loyalty programs and good service, and gaining new ones from their referrals.
GRO-01.New distribution channels: Selling through additional routes to the customer, such as wholesalers, other retailers or direct sales.
GRO-01.Vertical integration: Taking over another stage of the supply chain: buying a supplier (backward integration) or a distributor or retailer (forward integration).
GRO-01.Upselling and cross-selling: Raising the value of each sale by persuading customers to buy a better version (upselling) or related extra items (cross-selling).
GRO-01.Horizontal integration: Buying or merging with a competitor at the same stage of the supply chain, such as one bakery buying another.
GRO-01.Government contracting: Winning contracts to supply goods or services to government agencies, which are large and reliable customers.

GRO-02.Sell the business: The owner sells the whole company to an outside buyer, such as a competitor or larger firm, and receives the price in return.
GRO-02.Initial public offering: The company sells its shares to the public on a stock exchange for the first time, letting the owners turn their holdings into cash over time.
GRO-02.Family succession: The owner hands the business on to children or other relatives, by gift, sale or inheritance, keeping it in the family.
GRO-02.Merger: The business combines with another company to form one firm. The owner receives cash or shares in the combined company.
GRO-02.Liquidation: The owner closes the business, sells its assets, pays its debts and keeps whatever money remains.
GRO-02.Management buyout: The company's own managers buy the business from the owner, often using borrowed money.
GRO-02.Sell to a partner: A co-owner buys the departing owner's share. A buy-sell agreement written in advance often sets the price and terms.
GRO-02.Bankruptcy: A legal process for a business that cannot pay its debts. Under court supervision it is either closed and its assets sold, or reorganized.
GRO-02.Employee stock ownership plan: A trust set up to buy the owner's shares on behalf of the employees, who gradually become the owners of the company.
GRO-02.Private equity buyout: An investment firm buys the company, usually aiming to grow or reorganize it and sell it again later at a profit.
GRO-02.Leveraged buyout: A purchase of the company paid for mostly with borrowed money, with the company's own assets and cash flow used to secure and repay the loans.
GRO-02.Acquihire: A larger company buys a small one mainly to gain its talented employees, not its product, which is often shut down.
GRO-02.SPAC merger: The business merges with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), a shell already listed on a stock exchange, and so becomes public without a normal offering.
GRO-02.Recapitalization: Changing the mix of debt and ownership in the company, for example by borrowing or selling part of it, so the owner takes cash out while keeping a stake.

GRO-03.Exporting: Making the product at home and selling it to buyers in another country. It is the lowest-risk way in, as little is invested abroad.
GRO-03.Franchising: Granting a business in the foreign country the right to operate outlets under the brand and system, in return for fees and royalties.
GRO-03.Licensing: Allowing a foreign company to make or sell the product, or use the brand or technology, in return for a royalty.
GRO-03.Joint venture: Forming a jointly owned business with a company in the foreign country, combining the entrant's product with the partner's local knowledge.
GRO-03.Foreign direct investment: Putting money into owning facilities in another country, such as building a factory or opening stores there. It gives control but carries high risk.
GRO-03.E-commerce: Selling to foreign customers through a website or international online marketplace, without setting up a physical presence there.
GRO-03.Strategic alliance: A cooperation agreement with a foreign company, for example to share distribution or technology, without forming a new jointly owned firm.
GRO-03.Wholly owned subsidiary: A company in the foreign country that the parent firm owns 100 percent. Building it from scratch is called a greenfield investment.
GRO-03.Acquisition: Buying an existing company in the foreign country, which gives immediate access to its customers, staff and facilities.
